^'DEPORTATION ORDERS, MENTALLY ILL IMMIGRANTS

1. When misfortune befalls a landed immigrant requiring temporarv admittance to a mental hos-

pital, does the Department of Citizenship and Immigration issue an order for deportation to the immigrant's country of origin?
2.	When the immigrant regains his health and he is at no time a charge to the state and is allowed to remain in Canada, and he applies for citizenship, does the order of deportation prevent him from qualifying?
3.	How long has he got to wait before the order of deportation is removed?
4.	Is there any discretionary power vested in the minister, deputy minister, or in any other official of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to remove a deportation order?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
1. Section 19 (1) (e) (iii) of the Immigration Act requires that a report be submitted to the director of immigration on any person, other than a Canadian citizen or a person with Canadian domicile, who among other things becomes an inmate of an asylum or hospital for mental diseases. The director may, if he considers such action warranted, order that an immigration special inquiry be held to determine whether the individual is subject to deportation. If an inquiry is not ordered, the individual retains his status and may acquire citizenship in due course. Should an inquiry take place and deportation be ordered, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration may suspend deportation and allow the person concerned to stay in Canada under special authority. Rarely is anyone deported because of mental illness unless it is clearly in his interest to be returned to his own country.
2. With the issuance of a deportation order, the process of acquiring Canadian domicile automatically ceases and, without domicile, an individual is not eligible to qualify for Canadian citizenship. The passage of time does not affect the validity of a deportation order and so long as the order remains in force, the individual cannot qualify for citizenship.
3 and 4. Neither the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the deputy minister nor any other official of the department has any discretion to cancel or quash a deportation order properly based on provisions of the act, although the minister may direct at any time that an inquiry be reopened for the purposes of receiving any additional evidence which could affect the special inquiry officer's original decision. Unfortunately, as the Immigration Act now stands, it is not possible to reinstate the landed immigrant status of a person ordered deported on mental grounds even though he may have recovered. This is one of the problems which is to be dealt with in the revision of the Immigration Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
1. Control of the sale or distribution of new drugs is provided by sections C.08.001 to C.08.009, inclusive, of the food and drug regulations. The general distribution of a new drug may not be undertaken until the requirements of section C.08.002 are met. Limited distribution to qualified investigators for the sole purpose of clinical testing may be undertaken only when the manufacturer has filed with the food and drug directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare a preclinical submission in satisfactory form and content containing the information prescribed by section C.08.005.
2.	Tests to establish the value and safety of a drug are required both before and during clinical investigation. Before clinical investigation may be undertaken, a manufacturer is required by section C.08.005 of the regulations to provide, amongst other data, information concerning the results of investigations made to support the clinical use for the new drug, contraindications and precautions known in respect thereof and the suggested treatment of overdosage, concerning methods, equipment, plant and controls used in the manufacture, processing and packaging of the drug, detail of tests applied to control the potency, purity and safety of the drug, as well as the name and qualifications of investigators to whom the drug is to be distributed and the names of all institutions in which it is proposed further investigations be carried out.
3.	Since no formal preclinical submission has been filed to date with the food and drug directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare on a preparation designated as anablast serum, no formal investigation of the case has been made by the department.
4.	The officials of the food and drug directorate frequently hold ad hoc meetings with

Canadian specialists. In addition the Canadian drug advisory committee is consulted on matters concerning drugs.
5.	The Minister of National Health and Welfare is responsible for the final decision as to whether the manufacturer of a new drug has complied with the regulations.
6 and 7. The sections of the food and drug regulations dealing with new drugs, as part of the over-all food and drug legislation, is legislation in the field of criminal law and the prohibitions contained therein are statutory prohibitions, the violation of which may lead to prosecution. Decisions of the minister in respect thereof are therefore subject to test through the normal process of law.
8.	Until more information is available on anablast serum no decision can be reached as to whether it would be an appropriate subject for referral to the special committee on food and drugs.

Up until now, the discussions indicate that, on the whole, participating countries are in favour of those objectives. However, there is disagreement on the approach to take concerning certain proposals and it will be difficult to reconcile the various points of view during the next few weeks.
3.	Canada has been elected as one of the vice chairmen of the conference and our delegation plays an active and, I feel, a constructive role in the proceedings of the various committees. Canada's position was set out in a statement I made during the ministerial

meeting at the opening of the conference. The text of that statement is as follows: Following is the text of a statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Hon. Paul Martin, to the United Nations conference on trade and development in Geneva on Tuesday, March 24, 1964.
I wish to begin by congratulating you upon your election as president of this conference. I am confident that you will guide our deliberations over *the next few weeks toward constructive solutions on the many difficult and complex questions before us.
We are faced today with one of the great opportunities of the twentieth century. Throughout the world, governments and peoples expect this meeting to make definite progress toward a goal which each nation shares-the greater welfare of its people. We must never lose sight, in the long and complex debate, of the urgency of our responsibilities.
All of us recognize that this is an historic Conference. It is unprecedented in the breadth of participation and the nature of its objectives. The ability of our United Nations to respond to the needs of member countries is once again being tested. In recent weeks the United Nations and its member governments have been preoccupied with the organization's peace keeping role-and specifically with the critical situation in Cyprus. During this crisis, Canadians have, as our Prime Minister has said, been proud to play their full part once again. Mr. President, Canada can also be counted on to respond in those areas which are the objectives of this conference. We recognize that prosperity and stability are indivisibly linked.
Since its foundation, the United Nations has played an important and constructive role in the vital sector of economic and trade co-operation among nations. Member countries have joined together to dismantle the barriers to world trade with the aim of ensuring the best use of the world's resources and raising the living standards of the world's peoples. In the interests of expanding world trade, rules have been fashioned as safeguards against the restrictive and discriminatory practices of the past. The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the international monetary fund, the international bank and other United Nations institutions were set up to buttress the new framework of world trading relationships. This new and more liberal trade system has brought benefits to all the countries of the world. No country is more indebted to these accomplishments than my own, which is so vitally dependent on foreign trade. Canada supports the preservation and development of the basic trade rules and institutions which have been fashioned over the past two decades.
A great co-operative endeavour over the past two decades has been the economic development of new countries and countries seeking to reach new economic and social goals. The United Nations and its agencies have not only aroused world support for these efforts, but have also given us many of the tools to work with. Massive resources have been transferred by way of aid directly and through international agencies to reinforce even greater efforts of the developing countries themselves. That the efforts of these countries are bound to be paramount was emphasized yesterday in your own speech, Mr. President, when you pointed out that in this "endeavour for rapid economic growth to offset the increase in population and to keep up with the development
Questions
trends in advanced countries, the developing countries bear the main responsibility for their economic and social progress''. The same point was made by the present Prime Minister of Canada some years ago when he was speaking of the role of external aid. He went on, however, to develop this point in the following way: "The fact that external aid may often be marginal does not, however, make it unimportant. Many a garment might unravel if it were not for the hem. In much the same way, the fabric of economic and social life in many of these countries is strengthened by the function which outside assistance performs and by the evidence which it brings of widespread interest, sympathy and support."
Since the war Canada has made substantial contributions to international development efforts. From the start Canada actively encouraged the formation of United Nations programs and we backed up our support with substantial contributions. We were among the founding members of the Colombo plan in 1950 and since then we have annually transferred Canadian resources to countries in South and Southeast Asia, and more recently to Africa and countries in the Caribbean area. Through Canadian and United Nations programs we have provided substantial development resources, by far the greater part of which has been on a grant basis requiring no repayment.
The Canadian aid effort is part of a broad cooperative endeavour to hasten economic and social progress throughout the world. My government recognizes both the new sense of urgency behind this endeavour and the growing determination to achieve development goals. We have therefore decided to increase Canada's economic aid by more than one half. Our expanded effort includes a new program of long term loans on liberal terms. We expect our aid expenditures during the next months to reach $180 to $190 million.
Until recently the main emphasis in international arrangements has been to promote economic development through financial and technical assistance. We must now add another dimension to the great effort to support economic development. We must examine how trade can make a fuller contribution. The developing countries are rightly seeking through trade expansion to accelerate their economic development and to raise their living standards. World trade is still too much fettered by restrictions, high tariffs, trade discrimination and other barriers. The terms of trade have deteriorated for exporters of raw materials and foodstuffs. These basic products, moreover, are subject to sudden and unforeseen price fluctuations which can result in serious setbacks for development plans and for the efforts of producing countries. The developing countries are rightly seeking to diversify their economies, to create soundly based processing and manufacturing industries and to sell the products of these industries in the markets of the world. Their efforts deserve and require the encouragement of advanced countries. All of these countries represented here today stand to gain by increases in the productive capacity and prosperity of the less-developed world. As I see it, the task before this conference should be the establishment of a framework of world trade in which developing countries can achieve a satisfactory rate of economic growth and improved standards of living.
To achieve all these objectives will not be easy and will require adjustments and fresh efforts by all of us. Our task will be eased if we work together and share in the inevitable adjustments. By acting together within the United Nations, we can create in all our countries conditions and

Questions
the political will necessary for progress. Indeed, the only way to move forward effectively is by joint action.
Mr. President, the issues before this conference have been ably analysed in the report presented by the secretary-general, Dr. Haul Prebisch. His report presents us with many challenging proposals. I should like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to the distinguished services which he has already rendered to this conference.
My government-and I am sure each of the governments represented here-has given most serious thought to the issues facing this conference. Each of us will be making a contribution to the consideration of these problems in the days ahead. It may be helpful if I were to outline at this preliminary stage in a more specific way the Canadian approach on how these objectives can best be attained.
Canada will work with other developed countries in eliminating, wherever practicable, tariffs and other restrictions which obstruct trade in tropical foodstuffs and industrial raw materials traditionally exported by developing countries. The new round of tariff negotiations coming up in the GATT, known as the "Kennedy round", will complement this conference. These negotiations should reduce or eliminate barriers to many important exports from developing countries. To free world trade in food and raw materials would be a major accomplishment from which all countries in the world will benefit. At present Canada has no quantitative restrictions on imports of products of interest to developing countries and our tariffs on tropical products and raw materials are generally low or have been removed altogether; we have no internal taxes inhibiting the consumption of these products.
Canada has been a party to all major commodity agreements concluded since the end of the last war. We have always been prepared to explore with other countries the possibility of other agreements on a commodity by commodity basis. However, it would not be in the interest of the developing countries to encourage unduly high prices for primary commodities. High prices are likely to generate unsaleable surpluses by stimulating production and reducing consumption through the use of natural or synthetic substitutes.
Canada will work with the developing countries and others in trying to improve the conditions of world trade for temperate agricultural products. Agricultural protectionism in certain developed countries has been growing; it is tending to increase uneconomic production in these countries. It has curtailed the markets of efficient suppliers in developed and developing countries alike.
Canada had advocated that, in the forthcoming Kennedy round of tariff and trade negotiations, developed countries should ensure that products of interest to developing countries, including manufactured goods and semi-processed materials, are included in the scope of negotiations. As has been recognized in the GATT, this should be done without expecting full reciprocity from developing countries for benefits they may derive from these negotiations. We are hopeful also that successful negotiations of reduction of tariffs on semi-processed materials will go a long way to reducing differentials between tariffs on raw and processed commodities which have created problems for developing countries.
Canada strongly supports a general removal of quantitative restrictions now impeding imports into developed countries of manufactured goods from developing countries. It has been noted that exports of manufactures by developing countries are of limited variety and are exported in volume to only a few markets. Developing countries need the greatest possible freedom of access to the widest

number of markets if they are to establish a diversified and expanding industrial structure. The likelihood of market disruption would be lessened if these exports were less unevenly distributed among developed countries through the establishment of more uniformly favourable conditions of access.
While Canada is approaching the question of preferences with caution, we would be prepared to consider proposals for the exchange of regional tariff preferences among developing countries for a limited period of time and under conditions which took reasonable account of the interests of outside countries.
Canada would be prepared during the course of the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations to examine carefully any tariff preferences now enjoyed by Canada in the markets of the developing countries which may be regarded as prejudicial to the trade of other developing countries.
Canada recognizes that development plans and efforts may be prejudiced by adverse changes in the terms of trade or by other occurrences beyond the control of developing countries. Accordingly, we supported the recent decision of the international monetary fund to increase its help to countries suffering from temporary declines in export receipts. As regards longer term declines, we are prepared to join with others at this conference in studying ways of improving bilateral aid programs and relating them more closely to the changing economic and trading circumstances of the individual developing countries.
As regards the basic question of future institutional arrangements, it is our belief that we can only see clearly what will be required when we approach the end of our deliberations. We shall then have a better idea of what is likely to emerge as a result of the conference. In general, we are not in favour of setting up a new organization of a more or less independent character. Rather we would be more inclined to adapt the existing machinery to make it more responsive to the problems of the developing countries. Indeed encouraging progress is already being made in that direction.
This, Mr. President, is the position of the Canadian delegation at the outset of this conference. It will be clear from my presentation that we believe that much more can be done and must be done to free the channels of trade. We think that, if this were done, the developing countries would have a better opportunity of competing on terms which would bring into play their natural advantages as efficient producers of certain commodities and manufactures. The freeing of trade channels would also help to overcome the effects of undue protectionism in the developed countries and to lead of itself to some of that international division of labour to which reference has already been made in this conference. But I do not want to suggest that the freeing of the channels of trade is all that requires to be done. The range of problems which we have come to consider is vast and no single nor simple solution for them is likely to be possible. We are prepared, Mr. President, to join others at this conference in exploring patiently all avenues along which solutions may lie. We have come to listen to the views and preoccupations of others as much as to share with them our experiences as a young and expanding country.
The object of the conference, as we see it, will be to contribute to the solution of problems which are crucial to the well-being of a very large proportion of the human race. They are urgent problems and their solution is urgent. Many new nations have come into being over the past decade

or so. Their governments are concerned-as they must be concerned-to ensure that the political independence they have achieved should find fruition in rising standards of living, in better health and improved opportunities for education, and in the greater happiness of all their people. The urgency of this task is such that they cannot accomplish it by themselves. The more developed countries must come to their aid-as indeed they have already come to their aid-recognizing that in a world which is becoming daily more interdependent, the conditions under which mankind lives will have to be brought into a more equitable relationship. It has been said of the people of the developing countries that they were embarked on a "revolution of rising expectations". It is to take a step forward in the direction of meeting these expectations, Mr. President, that this conference has been called and I am glad to be able to pledge the active co-operation of the Canadian delegation in the work in which we are about to engage.

speechtext: have a question for the Associate Minister of National Defence. speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Cardin (Associate Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: ARTS. LETTERS AND SCIENCES ATTENDANCE AT ROYAL COMMISSION HEARINGS BY MEMBERS OF PUBLIC SERVICE AND ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
I am now in a position to answer the hon. member's question and to inform the house that there is no prohibition, first, against civil servants appearing before the royal commission on biculturalism and bilingualism and giving evidence if they wish to do so. No instructions have been issued by the Department of National Defence which would question this right.
Concerning members of the armed forces, the Queen's regulations preclude a member of the forces giving public evidence on a military subject or publishing in writing, or delivering any lecture, address or broadcast in any way dealing with a subject of a controversial nature pertaining to public policy without permission of headquarters. Army headquarters sent a message on May 4 to its commands as a reminder of these provisions.
Due to the special nature of this inquiry, however, it is recognized to be in the public interest that the widest range of views and opinions should be obtained, including those of the members of the forces. It is nevertheless important, having regard to the problems associated with military discipline, that arrangements be available which will give individual members of the forces the opportunity to present views freely if they so wish without compromising that discipline. The commission has agreed in these circumstances to receive evidence of any members of the forces who so desire, in camera. The Department of National Defence will cooperate in encouraging the attendance of members of the forces who wish to appear before the commission.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thought it might be helpful if I gave a general outline of the proposals contained in the estate tax resolution before the committee begins to consider them in detail.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. It is a little difficult for the Chair to hear what is being said by the hon. member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The resolution is divided into five paragraphs that outline the most important of the changes proposed for the Estate Tax Act. In addition the bill to amend the act will contain several other useful amendments.
Paragraph 1 implements part of the proposal made to the provinces last November to leave to them a larger share of the death duties field. It provides for a 75 per cent abatement, instead of the existing 50 per cent abatement, of the federal estate tax otherwise payable in respect of property in a province that levies a succession duty. The 75 per cent abatement will apply only to British Columbia

at present because the other two provinces that levy a succession duty, Ontario and Quebec, have chosen not to raise their rates at present but to qualify instead for an equivalent tax abstention payment of 25 per cent. The existing 50 per cent abatement will continue to apply in respect of property situated in Ontario and Quebec. The existence of two levels of abatement will require a consequential amendment to the rules determining the situs of property.
Paragraph 2 proposes that the amount of certain kinds of property, such as money on deposit, that may be transferred from the deceased's estate to a beneficiary without the consent of the Minister of National Revenue be increased to $2,500 from $1,500 for each transferor. It also proposes that an amount of $2,500 payable under an insurance policy for sickness or accident may also be transferred without the minister's consent. These proposals are intended to make a greater amount of cash readily available to beneficiaries while the estate is being settled.
The next three paragraphs are concerned with amendments to correct anomalies or deficiencies in the law. Paragraph 3 deals with a special kind of settlement and is intended to ensure that such settlements will be taxed on the same basis as other settlements. Paragraph 4 also deals with a special kind of transfer-a disposition out of community property-and is intended to provide more uniform and equitable tax treatment. The proposal in paragraph 5 is intended to prevent the use of tax avoidance devices.
These proposals, and several others, will be found in the amending bill, and are those that it seemed necessary or appropriate to recommend to parliament at this time. I should like to reiterate, however, a statement made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, as reported at page 980 of Hansard for March 16, 1964:
In reviewing the Estate Tax Act in the light of the representations that had been made about it, I was impressed with the case made by women's organizations saying that more recognition should be given to the special contribution that a wife makes to the accumulation of property by her husband. Any action to give effect to suggestions of this nature, however, would now affect provincial revenues more than our own budget position. Death duties are under review by provincial commissions of inquiry as well as by our royal commission on taxation. We have therefore deferred any action on this matter, and hope that there will be consultations with the provinces on it, as well as on other aspects of death duties, following the reports of the various commissions.

I have a few points I should like to make at this time, particularly with regard to the statement made by the parliamentary secretary in respect of the words of the Minister of Finance appearing at page 980 of Hansard for March 16. I am just wondering
Estate Tax Act
what the minister meant by saying that he was much impressed with the case made by women's organizations that more recognition should be given to the special contribution a wife makes to the accumulation of property by her husband. We know many organizations have sought an increase in the basic exemption of an estate from $60,000 or $70,000 to $80,000. I will say that I agree there is a rather difficult position now that the federal government has more and more handed over the revenue from the estate tax to the provinces. It would be rather difficult for the federal government to suggest now that it would increase the exemption ceiling without the consent of the provinces. In other words, the federal government would actually be giving away provincial money. This is a very difficult position in which to find one's self.
However, I find it difficult to reconcile this statement with some other statements that have been attributed to the Minister of Finance to the effect that Canadians will undoubtedly face an increase in taxation as a result of these concessions or allocations of sources of revenue to the provinces. I do not believe the minister can have it both ways. I am a little dubious about the sincerity of his statement. While it sounds nice, I think the minister's freedom of action is very limited, and the best interpretation I can put on the budget statement is that it was a pious hope.
I should like to know what further information has been received by the government of Canada as a result of any studies that have been made by provincial bodies or by the royal commisison on taxation. I am referring now to the last sentence in the minister's statement which appears at the top of the second column of page 980 of Hansard.
Turning now to the resolution as it appears before us, I wonder if the parliamentary secretary can give us a little more detail as to the effect of the British Columbia legislation to which the minister referred at the time of the budget, and which has now had the effect of setting up two scales of valuation or abatement. I leave that point with a request for information.
In so far as paragraph 2 of the resolution is concerned, which increases the ceiling on permissible transfers by a representative of a deceased person, I should like to refer to joint bank accounts and also to land held under joint tenancy. I have always been bothered by the application of the estate tax or the succession duty on the legal position resulting from the death of a joint tenant. For purposes of taxation it has always been deemed that half the value of the property shall have been assessed to the deceased. This

Estate Tax Act
is a new legal definition given to joint tenancy for reasons of the estate tax. I know that this is contained in the number of judgments of various taxation bodies. I have always found these to go rather hard against the legal interpretation of joint tenancy.
I must find that in the provinces where there is a land registry system which recognizes joint tenancies. This is a fact in connection with the majority of new homes being bought in these provinces where the mortgage companies insist on joint title to have both husband and wife on the mortgage for additional protection. All that is required is the filing of a death certificate to vest the title in the survivor. I am wondering how, in the field of property rights, the crown of Canada through the Estate Tax Act purports to interrupt or impede such a vesting of title without the consent of the minister. I trust the parliamentary secretary may have an answer to this question. How can the minister require that a provincial act shall be affected when there is a legal consequence flowing from the decease of a joint tenant? He may have an answer, and I would be most interested in it.
It is true that the amendment in paragraph 2 of this resolution will increase the ceiling on the property that may be permitted to pass without the consent of the minister. The additional portion, I think, is quite reasonable in that it provides for a certain amount payable under an insurance policy in respect of sickness or accident, in which a deceased had a beneficial or other interest immediately prior to his death. I can see that this will facilitate the payment of hospital bills immediately, by the representative or widow of a deceased, or by whoever may take on that responsibility. This is a move in the right direction.
However, with regard to those provinces where there is registration of the minister's certificate prior to an actual transfer of property, I would like to ask, have there been consultations with the provinces in regard to the increase of the ceiling from $1,500 to $2,500? I remember that this was a matter which was discussed some four or five years ago.
With respect to paragraph 4 of the resolution I wonder whether the inclusion of the words "out of any community of property" is limited to the province of Quebec, which is the only province in which the term "community of property" really applies, or whether this is dealing with joint tenancies, which I would submit is a form of community ownership of property. Is it only with respect to the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.

Very well, that clears up that point. Now, with respect to paragraph 5 I know that this matter of these very complex schemes has exercised the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue for some time, particularly where they seem to defeat the purpose of the act. Under these circumstances perhaps the parliamentary secretary could give us some indication of the type of thing aimed at, without necessarily going into all the details.
I would ask him to give us as much information as he can at this time because this is a relatively new act and we have not had long experience of it. We are not getting, shall we say, too many progress reports, which may be expected in the long run. Since the act has only been in force for five years the committee and the country would appreciate receiving an estimation of how it is working out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps I should deal with some of the questions raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West before further questions are raised by other members. The first matter which he mentioned was the question raised by the minister of giving further recognition to the contribution of women towards the building up of an estate. In this regard representations have been made for a number of years by women's organizations. The matter was considered very seriously by the minister at the time of his budget preparation, but it was decided that it would be unfair, as was pointed by the hon. member for Edmonton West, for the federal government to legislate in a manner which would materially affect the amount of revenue derived from the estate tax, in that 75 per cent of this revenue goes to the provinces.
This also affects other matters under the Estate Tax Act, and I believe in the future that amendments to the act which materially affect the amount of revenue which it raises will have to be made after due consultation with the provinces because, after all, they get 75 per cent of the amount of money which is raised by it.
In the case of the differences which arose and are covered in paragraph 1, in British Columbia the provincial government decided to take up the 25 per cent room which the federal government agreed to vacate last year, and it amended its legislation and raised the rates of the succession duty levied in that province accordingly. I can assure the hon. member that it is not within the jurisdiction of the department to decide whether they have exactly taken it up, or taken it up more or less. I would not like to give an opinion

on this, but they have legislated to take up the differential and no special treatment was required.
In the case of Ontario and Quebec they have not as yet amended their legislation and have chosen instead to take a 25 per cent abatement of the tax collected by the federal government, pending the time when they will pass legislation to move into the field to the extent that the federal government has moved out of it.
With respect to the question raised by the hon. member on paragraph 2, this does not affect joint tenancy in real property in that the section which is being amended, section 47(3) of the act, does not cover real property. Therefore joint tenancy in real property does not enter into this particular matter. While the hon. member was speaking I think I mentioned that the amendment with respect to community property was designed primarily for the situation in Quebec, and I understand it is the same treatment as that which is given under the Succession Duty Act in the province of Quebec.
The hon. member asked how the act is working and I am informed by officials of the Department of National Revenue that since its enactment the Estate Tax Act has been working very well.

I make apologies to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) but it will not take me long.
Looking at the estimates concerning the Estate Tax Act, we realize once again that the civil servants' jargon is very hard to understand; thus, when poor people die, leaving their family in want, one has to resort to experts in order to understand what it is all about and be informed of the heirs' obligations towards the government.
Reading the amendments to the act introduced today-of course, I am not an expert and I am not bright either-I find it is very difficult to know exactly what is the meaning of some clauses and what is involved in those clauses we are going to vote in a moment and agree to practically unanimously.
I think this is a failure on the part of our democratic and private enterprise systems. We have reached a point where we do not know where we stand or where we are going. We are dependant on a group of people whose activity is outside their field of interests, and it is difficult to understand their directives.
I think it is a little paradoxical that where a system like ours which pretends to defend democracy and free enterprise as compared to socialist dictatorship, would take steps to
Estate Tax Act
ensure that we reached, at the same time, a point where we defend private enterprise on the one hand, and on the other, we promote the intrusion of socialistic measures which bring with them a multitude of incomprehensible rules, such as those we have before us at this time.
Naturally, if one tries to understand those amendments, it appears that the government has decided to give back to the provinces a small share of the taxation powers on estates. Neither the federal nor the provincial governments seem to be able to do completely without the estates taxes which, in many cases, have reduced to poverty families which were fairly well off beforehand. In other words, those taxes have led numerous small and average businesses to bankruptcy because the government, seeing that it could not get the funds it needed while the owners were alive, succeeds in laying its hands on that money once they have passed away.
I must repeat what I said a moment ago: To my mind, it is a failure on the part of democracy.
If our businessmen and our governments do not try to find a means to simplify the legislation-really, Mr. Chairman, if you have the time to read this, you will probably ask what is it all about when you are through reading it. I would not blame you. A large proportion of the 265 members of the house are also surely in the dark.
Not so large.

It may not be so large, but there are many members of the house who surely do not know what it is all about. And yet we are obliged to vote and pass this legislation for otherwise, we are told, the government will be prevented from taking any action.
Mr. Chairman, I am not well versed in these matters, but without going into details, I think the legislation should be simplified as soon as possible instead of trying to find formulas in a style which is hardly understandable. The French language, just like the English language, is usually understandable. But when you read the English or the French version of this legislation, you cannot understand much.
However, we would like that in practice, at least in the field of succession duties, 100 per cent of the revenue be handed over to the provinces.
I was amazed, a moment ago, to hear the parliamentary secretary say that Ontario and Quebec had refused to accept this 25 per cent of the estate tax at a time when, in the province of Quebec, the premier goes around saying that he wants 100 per cent of those

Estate Tax Act
succession duties, when in fact he has refused the 25 per cent to take it back in the form of a general tax abatement.
Of course, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) shakes his head in disagreement but as far as I am concerned, that is the way I interpreted the statement made a while ago by the parliamentary secretary.
So, I repeat that the wording of this legislation is very hard to make out and I hope that before long we will have a government that will know how to draft legislation in more simple terms.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps I might answer one or two of the points raised by the hon. member. He has indicated that this legislation is difficult for the layman to understand, and I think that is generally the case with respect to taxation legislation. But I should like to point out that the present Estate Tax Act which was enacted a few years ago was regarded as a simplification of the act which it replaced, and is generally recognized as being a much simpler measure to deal with than was the former legislation on this subject.
With regard to the 75 per cent shared with the provinces, estate tax also enters the equalization payments; so that in effect we are giving to the provinces more than 75 per cent of the money collected from estate taxes.

I am in entire accord with the previous speaker. This is a complicated subject and I believe we are being a little optimistic when we ask for too much simplification, or, should I say oversimplification, in a field which is, after all, highly technical. As the parliamentary secretary has stated, we are already dealing with a simplification of the previous act.
I think it is only fitting that in recognizing the needs of the provinces the succession duty tax per se should be the first one vacated to the provinces under present conditions. I do not wish to enter too deeply into technical matters myself or to become involved with constitutional questions, but it certainly seems to me that succession duty is a tax on property, and very often a tax on real property which in so many ways falls under provincial jurisdiction. I think most hon. members interested in this field recognize that this is so, and while we are of necessity vacating certain tax fields at a time when the provinces are facing an increased burden on their resources, it seems we must agree in great measure with paragraph one and with the government's intention primarily to vacate this particular field.

I should like at this time to call attention to a more specific question, one which was touched upon by the hon. member who has just spoken. I do not intend to speak for very long but I feel obliged to bring this matter up in the house this afternoon. I know that the department has for many years been aware of this general problem. They are certainly seized of it and I am sure they will be aware of it for years to come. I draw attention to it now because the party which I support is a party which believes in a property-owning democracy; we think government should do all it can to encourage the ownership of property. As hon. members know, many families who own small businesses are obliged to let their holdings pass into other hands because of the necessity of raising succession duty quickly. I realize it is not always desirable that a company or an enterprise should be held by a family from one generation to another. But I am thinking particularly, now, not of large companies with many shares on the public market, but of small businesses which have been built up over the years. I am thinking, for example, of a small store owner who has very little in his patrimony except his business. But he has dependants, and they wish to carry on the business, but they are obliged to get rid of it because of the necessity of raising succession duty.
This is not a new problem and I believe some progress has been made in this regard in the past, but I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary to what extent provision can be made to alleviate the situation. Very often, companies are taken over by outside interests simply because succession duties cannot be raised within the time required. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that the question I am raising is not a new one and certainly has not any political overtones; but I am raising it because my party supports the principle of a property owning democracy. I think we in this house should do all we can to encourage people to own their own businesses, small or otherwise, and should not unnecessarily hang this cloud over their heads if anything can be done to avoid it.
While there is no one paragraph in the resolution before us today which deals specifically with this matter-it perhaps deals too generally with the subject-I would like to have a statement from the parliamentary secretary regarding this problem in general. I know the fact that we vacate these taxes to the provinces means that it is certainly not the federal government alone that can act to alleviate the situation; but surely the federal government, in so far as it is still in the succession duty field, has a role, with the provinces, to play in bringing about what

I think-I am not going to detail my remarks with any specific data at the present time- could be a solution to this problem. General information to which I have access leads me to believe that the problem is still a very real one at the present time and is deserving of further study in order that amendments or changes may be brought about to encourage family ownership and other types of ownership of small and even larger businesses; to encourage, in other words, the ownership of property.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks following upon those made by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, because we in this group believe in legitimate, responsible, private enterprise where there is no degree of exploitation of the community or the nation. I raise this point at the request of a number of constituents who have been faced with unexpected problems in recent years. Many persons are expressing concern because they were not affected a few years ago but are affected now. I refer particularly to heirs of farmers, the owners of small family industries and small businesses, and persons of that type.
I think this situation has largely come about as the result of the general increase in land and property values, which very often have little effect on the actual operation of the farm. There has been little increase in real wealth as far as the farm is concerned, but property values established as the result of developments in the district, or because of an increase in general property assessments in the area in which the small industry or business is located, have created this problem. Because of this situation, which has developed quite rapidly in the last ten years, a number of persons, the heirs of farmers, the heirs of persons operating small industries or small businesses, have been suddenly faced with an unexpected demand for estate taxes. I am not blaming the federal or provincial governments in this respect. However, it does come as a shock, and I have known a few cases where because of this valuation of properties people have been forced to sell a farm which had been in the family for generations and which they would have liked to carry on, or they have been forced to sell a small business.
I am thinking now of one case in my district of quite a successful farmer whose farm is worth say $175,000. If he were to die suddenly, his heirs would be faced with an unexpected demand for cash for estate tax, which I am quite certain they would not be able to meet and it would mean the sale of this family estate or farm. I am not speaking of a large property, but it is a valuable one because they produce fruit and the farm 20220-1901
Estate Tax Act
is located in the Arrow lakes district, which is so valuable for this purpose. A number of people have been to lawyers in the district to get a thorough explanation of the relationship between the federal estate tax and the succession duty tax in British Columbia. I have been told that even lawyers are baffled by the complicated nature of these relationships, and are sometimes unable to give a clear definition of just how the law would apply under certain circumstances. I understand that in order to overcome this difficulty gentlemen of the legal profession are advising their clients to incorporate, but in some cases they do not wish to do this and it does not meet the situation.
Following the remarks made by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, Mr. Chairman, we would like to hear the parliamentary secretary-who I know is most capable in matters of mathematics, economics, and that sort of thing, because these matters are within his particular field, and we recognize this-make a general statement on the policy with regard to estate tax and the policy of administration when it comes to the collection of estate tax from heirs of the type I have mentioned. Then I would like the parliamentary secretary to give, for the information of hon. members of the committee, a general resume of the provincial legislation in effect in each province in Canada and its relationship to the federal Estate Tax Act. I believe that is not asking too much on this very important question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the entire discussion of the two hon. members who have just spoken is out of order, in view of the resolution which is before the committee at the moment. However, I would refer them to Hansard of December 9 because-
Why?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think it is out of order because it does not deal with any of the particular items which are before the committee for amendment. However I would like to refer them to my statement in Hansard-

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, and just for clarification, I do not believe this discussion on the estate tax resolution is out of order. If I had found the necessary amendments in the resolution to alleviate the problem which I mentioned, perhaps I would not have had to raise the subject. Are we out of order, Mr. Chairman, when in general debate at the resolution stage we raise matters definitely relating to the Estate Tax Act, just because they are not included in the detailed clauses of the bill? I believe an hon. member is not out of order in the debate on the Estate Tax Act reso-

Estate Tax Act
lution when he raises problems which perhaps need to be dealt with under this heading.
I think we should have a clarification on this point at this time, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member wants a clarification I will have to tell him that a debate on an amending act does not open up discussion on the whole act, so that when we have before us certain specific and particular sections of a statute which are being considered in committee, we cannot discuss other sections of the statute which are not before the committee. I think this is generally recognized practice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I merely wish to bring this point to the attention of the committee. I would in this regard refer hon. members to my statement as reported in Hansard of December 9 in which I dealt with this particular problem in some detail.
I tried to deal with it fairly at that time. As a matter of fact, something of what I said was misinterpreted. I stated at that time that any decision that would allow people to pay their succession duties or estate taxes by instalments would of necessity require consultation with the provinces, which was interpreted as my being against such consultation, and of course I am not against it.
I think it is completely unfair for the hon. member for Kootenay West to want me to explain the implications of all the succession duty acts in Canada when dealing with this particular resolution.
There is a problem in connection with family businesses which exists in this field and, as hon. members know, the officials of the Department of National Revenue have been looking at this problem for some time. One of the great difficulties with which they have had to deal is the fact that nobody comes forward and gives us a specific example of a business which has had to be sold because of having to pay the estate tax. People talk of this generally but do not come forward and say that a particular business must be sold because of this.
Incidentally, with regard to the little farm in the Kootenays the hon. member was talking about-and I am sure farms are very valuable out there-which would be worth $175,000. On a quick calculation it seems to me that the person involved would have to pay approximately $22,000 in estate tax and succession duties. It would not seem to me impossible for such a person to be able to raise $22,000 with $175,000 as security. I am not in any way minimizing the arguments which have been put forward to the effect that there should be some way of paying

estate tax and succession duties on an instalment basis, and I am sure that when consultations take place with the provinces-and 1 believe consultations have to take place before major changes can be made-this matter will undoubtedly be discussed.

Mr. Chairman, just one last question on this point. I admit that it is rather difficult to get all this information immediately, but the minister is backed by an excellent and efficient staff. Could he provide hon. members with an outline of all the provincial legislation and its relationship to our Estate Tax Act? I think this is necessary because numbers of people are finding this matter very difficult; and this includes even the gentlemen of the legal profession who are supposed to know these matters.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order raised may I just make a reference to the fact that the preamble to this resolution reads in this way:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Estate Tax Act and to provide among other things:
-and so on. I do not think that there is a limitation here. I think that this is the sign of a government which I hope is prepared to listen to the excellent suggestions which flow from this side of the house; and it may be that when the bill following this resolution is introduced the suggestions which have been advanced from the opposition benches might receive consideration. We might find these suggestions reflected in the bill itself. Once the bill is before the house, then I do not think there is any question that we are limited to what is there; but with respect I would suggest that there is some leeway here, bearing in mind that the resolution does not purport to restrict the proposed amendments within the four corners of the five subparagraphs of the resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Without trying to make a general ruling the only thing I can do is to refer hon. members again to standing order 59 (2), which says that in committee discussion must be strictly relevant to the item before us. I would think that every specific contribution to the debate should be judged in the light of that standing order.

Mr. Chairman, if I understand correctly the proposed amendment to the Estate Tax Act, it changes very few things or a great many, depending on how you look at it.
Thus the amendment proposed in paragraph B of clause 1 would mean that the 75 per cent abatement is the result of the

federal-provincial agreements entered into at the federal-provincial conference held recently in Quebec or the conferences that followed one another in the past several years.
As pointed out so accurately by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux), we are faced with a torrent of words that make up a puzzle, that perhaps 25 hon. members can understand but that 235 do not understand at all and never will. In fact, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) admits himself that it is difficult to read, especially to understand. It reads well but it is hard to understand, he says. And he adds that the previous act was still more confused, in short more ambiguous.
Instead of introducing amendments of all kinds, they should go straight to the point and say: the federal government withdraws from one taxation field, so that a province can take it over. They should not come up as they do with a torrent of words such as those, in an effort to confuse further the Canadian people. Even lawyers would not make anything out of the terms used in the clause or amendment submitted to us.
For instance, clause 2 reads as follows:
That the limit of $1,500 on the amount of certain kinds of property passing on the death of a deceased person-be increased to $2,500-
There is no need for seven lines or so many meaningless words. For example, it is mentioned:
That the limit of $1,500 on the amount of certain kinds of property passing on the death of a deceased person-
This means the spouse. Everybody understands that.
-that may be transferred, delivered or paid over to any person resident in Canada without the consent of the minister, in the case of any one transferor, deliverer or payer, be increased to $2,500-
Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure the parliamentary secretary must have felt like laughing when he read that subsection or, rather, that sentence.
-and that such kinds of property be extended to include an amount payable under a policy of insurance in respect of sickness or accident in which the deceased had, immediately before his death, a beneficial or other interest.
Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the discussion, I should like the parliamentary secretary of the Minister of Finance to tell us flatly that the idea is to have the provinces take over that field of taxation from the federal authorities. There is nothing else. Let us not try to fool the public by saying that the tax rate or the succession duties rates which the federal government collected previously are being reduced.
Estate Tax Act
It is agreed between the central government and certain provinces, in this case Quebec, that the central government withdraws from that field of taxation so that the province of Quebec may collect the money which was previously collected by the federal government. There is absolutely no reduction of the tax. As a matter of fact, the people of Quebec will have to pay exactly what they were paying previously, if not more.
That is why I say that this measure is the result of the federal-provincial conference which was held in Quebec recently, and that is what I would like the parliamentary secretary to admit frankly, without any back door method and without mental reservation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think, in the circumstances, that I have to admit anything. I would remind the hon. member for Villeneuve that my statement on introducing these particular amendments was, I believe, quite clear. I said that the first paragraph of the resolution as presented is to implement the agreement which was arrived at with the provinces here in Ottawa. I stated that quite clearly. With regard to the number of words used in the particular amendment, I am not an expert on the use of a torrent of words but I am informed that it was necessary in the case of clause 2, the clause referred to by the hon. member, to use this number of words in order to tie it in correctly as an amendment to section 47 (3) of the Estate Tax Act.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks I should like to make. First of all, I think the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency expressed the thoughts of many of us on this Estate Tax Act. It is far too complicated for the ordinary person to understand. I think it is the right of the ordinary person who earns the money and pays the shot to have laws written so that he can interpret them.
Oh boy.

Someone says "Oh boy!", but I say this act is difficult to understand. The
same criticism is made in our profession___
that it is sometimes difficult to understand what we are saying. A language should be a communicable language so that the ordinary person can understand it, whether it be in the legal profession, the medical profession or any other profession.
Or the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

I should like to make the suggestion, although I may be wandering a little afield, that there should be a uniform estate

Estate Tax Act
tax throughout Canada. We hear talk about tax sharing agreements. I should like to know why in the world the various finance ministers across Canada cannot get together and work out something that will not be so complicated. Today we have the parliamentary secretary telling us that he cannot do anything because of provincial legislation. I say to him that it would add something to the unity of Canada if a national estate tax policy were adopted, and the government should start to work on it so that people across Canada will know where they stand, no matter in what province they live. Today people move from one province to another much more often than a few years ago.
I am wondering about the amount of $2,500 that may be transferred without the consent of the minister on the death of a person. I know this amount represents an increase and I want to compliment the government for increasing it. But surely $2,500 today is a pretty small amount when you consider that somebody who has been sick and has died will have incurred hospital bills over and above the amount provided for by hospital insurance. In addition there would be nurses' accounts to look after. The beneficiary has to live, eat and pay rent and other expenses. The result is that in a month or two all the money on hand is gone.
I know the parliamentary secretary will say that all such people have to do is to apply to the estate tax people and they will give them some money. However, this is at the whim of the officials. I do not say they are necessarily not going to rule reasonably, but they are quite far removed from the actual events and do not understand the whole problem, although they do the best they can. We know that the dollar is eroded every year by 2 or 3 per cent and therefore I suggest that to be realistic this amount should be $5,000 instead of $2,500.
I also want to say a few words on the matter of annuities. Not being a lawyer, I am not quite clear why this provision is not written so that I can understand it. However, let us say that a father buys an annuity for one of his sons and he pays for it in one lump premium. The annuity for his son or possibly his grandson comes due in 20 years. It may be an educational policy. What happens if the father or grandfather dies after 10 years? What is the difference in treatment with regard to an annuity if he is making yearly payments and has to pay 20 premiums?
I want to conclude my remarks by saying that I certainly feel badly that nothing can be done for women who have worked to build up estates. The husband passes on and the widow is not allowed any credit for what she has done in building up the husband's estate.

I think this is very bad. Some women can go out to work for 20 years and build up an estate, but the woman who stays at home on the farm or the woman who stays at home to raise her children until they get through high school is treated as if she has not done anything to build up her husband's estate.
I do not think that is right or fair and I am hoping that the government will do something about the matter. I hope something can be devised that will apply across Canada whereby women will be treated more fairly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should like to deal with a couple of the matters raised by the hon. member for Simcoe East. With regard to the point about the complexity of the Estate Tax Act, I stated earlier that the present act is really a simplification of the former succession duty act, and I can assure the hon. member that it is much simpler than the succession duty act was.
Perhaps we will get there yet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
With regard to aiding laymen in preparing succession duty returns, first of all I must remind the committee that someone leaving a widow has to have an estate amounting to $60,000 before any estate tax is payable. Usually these returns are handled by lawyers in the course of dealing with the estate as such. There is a four page guide for filing returns, which is available to anyone. It is almost a layman's guide to assist people in filing estate tax returns.
With regard to the matter of the $2,500, which is being raised from $1,500, it is $2,500 from each bank in which the deceased may have had an account, so it might amount to more than $2,500. If he had accounts in several banks, $2,500 could be paid out of each one of them. In addition, if he had a sickness or accident policy there would be another $2,500 available there. This amount is exactly the amount which was requested by the Canadian federation of business and professional women in their brief to the government on this particular matter.
I agree with the hon. member that it would be nice to have one estate tax act across the whole of Canada. Certainly I should like to see similar legislation all across Canada in regard to other statutes such as the Companies Act. I think something may be accomplished in this regard in that the recent federal-provincial conference agreed to set up a taxation committee to consider matters of taxation, and I certainly think that the question of a uniform estate tax act across the country could and perhaps should be considered by this group.

I dealt earlier with the problem of the recognition of the woman's part in contributing to the estate, and the Minister of Finance also dealt with this matter in his budget speech. I expressed the view that while the government felt something should be done to recognize, beyond the $60,000 exemption, the contributions of women to building up estates of deceased persons, it was felt that this could not be done until there had been consultation with the provinces, in that 75 per cent of the revenue arising out of the estate tax goes to the provincial governments.

Mr. Chairman, everyone in the house seems to hold the same feeling of great concern about succession duties or estate tax goes to the provincial governments, taxation between the provinces and the federal government, the hon. member for Simcoe East referred to a national estate tax policy and the parliamentary secretary answered that he would encourage such a move and hoped that there might be such a policy.
I see a great danger as more succession duty taxing power is placed in the hands of the provinces. We have had examples of tax havens in order to encourage people to move to such areas where there are no succession duties. The Bahamas are one area and Monaco is another.
I can appreciate the difficulties of the provinces in attempting to attract capital within their own boundaries. They might, in order to do this, reduce the amount of the succession duty and get into competition with one another in attempting to attract capital for their own provincial areas.
I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that, in so far as taxation is concerned, people do not have to live within boundaries of Canada. Today it is not necessary for someone to remain in Canada. Persons who build estates have the privilege of moving to an area in which there is no succession duty. I would agree with one of the earlier speakers, that there is today in Canada a process of liquidating family owned businesses in order to provide ready cash for succession duty purposes. This money could very well be used for the expansion of that business.
The parliamentary secretary referred to the possibility of establishing an instalment plan for the payment of these duties. This might very well be considered, or we might consider freezing the estate at a certain value. This might not be the time or the place to discuss this suggestion. However, I feel the parliamentary secretary should consider the suggestions that have been put forward today, one of which was the establishment of a national estate tax so there would be no
Estate Tax Act
difference in rate as between the provinces. If this trend continues, and one province is asking for 100 per cent of succession duties, I believe there should be a move to establish uniformity of succession duties as between the provinces.

I have a few remarks to make, plus one more question to ask. First of all, with regard to what the hon. member for York North had to say, I believe it was the motive of the previous administration in passing this Estate Tax Act to introduce some uniformity in estate tax matters across the country. I am speaking subject to correction, but I believe there are only three provinces at the present time who seem to pursue an independent succession duty policy. They are British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec. The other provinces work under this act and take a portion of the revenue derived therefrom. I think that it is a good model.
The hon. member for Simcoe East and the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, both of whom are practising physicians, criticized the lawyers for the drafting of this act. I find this rather paradoxical in view of the mysterious language of a medical certificate because, in my view, that is the absolute mystery of mysteries. Then, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency mentioned the plight of the poor person in dealing with this act. Since the death duties start when an estate is valued at $60,000 and the widow is given $10,000 for every dependant, I cannot feel that those concerned are entirely poor people. The hon. member may have been referring to some of the provincial acts about which I have no comments. When we are talking about the equality of women and the emancipation of women I may say, as an aside, that some people have suggested we should make an amendment to bring about an equality for men, because a male survivor is entitled to less consideration than is a widow, even though the income earning capacity has been on the side of the female partner to the marriage.
I am again concerned with paragraph 3. I should like the parliamentary secretary to advise me why it is, when there is included in the estate of a deceased the value of a life tenancy, that the life tenancy should be valued on the basis of the capital of the estate. Perhaps he could clear up this point. The way I interpret it, a life tenancy is valued on the basis of the estate from which it is paid, and I would have thought the life tenancy would be based on some sort of actuarial table and, in the case of a person who has died, this life tenancy should come

Estate Tax Act
to an end. I may have completely misunderstood the nature of the amendment, and I should like to have some clarification.
The last point I should like to make is one which arises from one of the complexities of the various succession duties acts, and that is the right of certain provinces to declare the situs of personal property. We may have a person who has lived all his life in Alberta and who has accumulated an estate including shares in a corporation whose head office is in the province of Ontario or Quebec. These two taxing authorities will, of course, exact their portion of the death duties in the case of the death of a person in Alberta, because the transfer agent of the company will require a clearance from the succession duty authority of the province of either, say Ontario or Quebec. I must confess this causes some problems in cases where there are multiple transfer agents. For the life of me, I cannot see how the provinces of Ontario or Quebec can say they have the right to levy succession duties on the estate of a person who has lived solely in the province of Alberta. The only connection with the province of Quebec, say, would be that the estate owns some shares in a company that happens to have its head office in Quebec and therefore succession duties have to be paid on that basis.
It is true that we may not be able to do much about this, but I think it is completely wrong. The valuation of the shares may be based on the operations of the company outside the province of Quebec, especially if it happens to be an interprovincial company. I am only using Quebec as an example, and I do not say that this province alone acts in this fashion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
First of all, I should like to deal with the two questions raised by the hon. member. Paragraph 3 deals with the taxation of the capital of a trust fund where the deceased has kept the income or reserved a benefit in the fund.
The problem of situs raised by the hon. member is a difficult problem. The position of the provinces in this regard is that the law which governs them arises out of the common law and they are not able to vary the common law. It arises out of decisions over the years, whereas the rules used by the federal government in the Estate Tax Act are statutory, although generally based on the common law.

I think it is the reverse. With the greatest respect I think so, in that the situs principle adopted by the provinces is that which applied to land, whereas the common law concerning personal property is

that personal property follows the domicile of the owner. But in these cases they have taken the real property principle, that is, that ownership of shares and taxability of shares should be governed by the situs of the head office.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am informed by the officials that what I stated a few minutes ago was correct, and that provincial situs of shares, which was the particular question raised, arises out of the common law, so that the situs is the point at which they are transferred rather than the point at which they are resting.

My question concerns paragraph 3. To my knowledge there are a good many estates that are left to a beneficiary for the lifetime of the beneficiary, and in most cases on the death of a beneficiary they go to children. Is it contemplated under this paragraph that the interest which, say, a widow has had in an estate for the period of her lifetime shall be included in property declared by her at her death?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The answer is no.
Because she would be taxed twice if that were the case.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The answer is no.
