speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill provides for the implementation, without change, of the proposals which were set out in detail in the budget resolutions, and which the committee of ways and means already has examined on an item by item basis.
There is not much I can say about the substance of this bill without repeating what has been said already when the resolutions

were considered in committee. For this reason my remarks will be brief and confined to the structure of the measure.
Hon. members will note that clause 1 of the bill provides that certain existing tariff items be struck out and that there be substituted therefor the revised items which are set out in detail in Schedule A. This schedule is divided into two parts which implement resolutions 1 and 3 respectively.
No doubt many hon. members will recall that resolution 1 dealt with a negotiated package of tariff items arising from two tariff board reports, and that resolution 3 proposed a mixed bag of miscellaneous amendments. All of these were relieving or clarifying provisions. We1 have already been through the list once. Accordingly I shall say no more about it, except to repeat that this miscellaneous group of proposals does not include a single tariff increase. This is not, of course, the case with the negotiated package set out in Part I of Schedule A. It is a selfbalancing package including both increases and reductions.
Clause 2 of the bill provides for the new drawback item that was proposed in resolution 2. It is as recommended by the tariff board in its report on reference 129, tableware and glassware for decorating.
Clause 3 of the bill is the coming into force provision and flows from resolution 4.
As I said earlier, this bill implements what was proposed in the tariff resolutions without any change of substance whatsoever. Indeed, even the changes of form are the minimum necessary in order to convert the resolutions into statutory form.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few points I would like to raise in regard to the detail under clause 1, and since I shall be dealing with the schedule, I might be permitted certain leniency in this respect so that we can clear up our discussion that much sooner. I am particularly concerned as to the implementation of the recommendations of the tariff board with regard to oil country goods, that is goods that may be manufactured in Canada under licence and which go into oil production.
These resolutions, as included by the Minister of Finance in his budget proposals, arose out of a reference to the tariff board of some years standing, and which covered not only goods entering into the production of oil and gas but also goods in connection with the mining industry. I was very pleased to see the present administration followed what I felt had been the philosophy of the previous administration in this regard. I say this because I think these provisions should, in the long run, provide our industry, not only in central Canada but in Alberta
Customs Tariff
with a strong shot in the arm. Canadian industry involved in the production of goods and machinery for the oil industry has been subject to a disproportionate tariff balance as compared with United States industry.
As we know, when the oil industry started in this country back about 1947 Canadian facilities for the manufacture of any of this equipment were practically non-existent. But with the passage of time various business concerns have branched out into this field of activity and other firms have been founded to engage in the manufacture of these goods, a number of them by specialists in this industry who had come from the United States or from the United Kingdom. We know that in several cities of western Canada, particularly in Calgary and Edmonton we now have an extensive secondary industry in this regard.
One of the first steps to be taken was the provision of tariff protection for the manufacture of sucker rods, and an extensive business was established in Edmonton as a result. As a matter of fact, one concern which had gone bankrupt was able to get back on its feet and is now a very successful enterprise. I should like to know whether the parliamentary secretary can advise as to what extent the government considers it possible to forecast an increase in the manufacture of oil country goods in Canada as a result of these steps. I am looking for some technical information which was, I believe, at the disposal of the previous minister of finance, in order to encourage the government to enter upon this type of change. If it is only done as a matter of course in answer to representations, one wonders why it is being done at all. I think it is obvious the government has felt that these steps will lead to an increase in the manufacture of oil country goods in this country, and maybe some yardstick could be given us.
With reference to the term "oil country goods" and item 491 as it appears in the first schedule, I should like to know whether this will include specialized equipment having to do with the development of tar sands. As we understand it, the production from tar sand will not come from wells-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit me to interrupt, this is dealt with specifically in item 492c of schedule A.

Oh yes. Then perhaps the hon. gentleman could tell us what margin of protection is now being given. There has, naturally, been an exchange of some concessions in bargaining to lead to these tariff changes, particularly in the most favoured nation category. Previously, if the goods were

Customs Tariff
of a class or kind not made in Canada, in the most favoured nations tariff category the rates could go from 22J per cent to free. Now there is a standard 10 per cent.
To turn to another matter, under item 492(d) we know that there will be permitted free entry into Canada of materials for use in the manufacture of goods set out in tariff items 491 and 492. I should like the parliamentary secretary to tell us why. If it is intended that there should be a moderate degree of protection to Canadian industry manufacturing the finished goods, then the person or firm providing the materials which enter into the manufacture of those goods should enjoy a similar degree of protection. Let us take bolted steel tanks. I do not know what level of tariff would be imposed on the sheet steel which goes into the manufacture of the tanks. But if my interpretation of 492(d) is right, a foreign manufacturer of sheet steel used for the manufacture of steel tanks would enjoy free entry into this country if he could bring in the material under the terms of this item 492(d). The Canadian manufacturer has a choice; he can obtain his steel either from a Canadian manufacturer or from abroad. Would the parliamentary secretary advise me whether my thinking on this has been correct-that the manufacturer or furnisher of materials entering into the manufacture of oil country goods does not derive the protection which is given to the manufacturer of goods as envisaged in these particular tariff changes?
I have one last question and it has to do with the purpose of item 848. The amendment reads:
Drilling bits, n.o.p., and parts thereof, for use In exploratory or discovery work in connection with, and development, depletion and production of, petroleum or natural gas wells.
These items are to be admitted free. I am wondering why drilling bits, which can be manufactured in Canada and which, I would feel are brought in under some other item which is covered by some form of duty, should now be admitted without liability for duty. These are the questions I have to raise in reference to the oil country items and if the parliamentary secretary would reply to them I think I am just about clear as to the others.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
First, as I mentioned in my introductory statement, the purpose of the first two resolutions is to implement the recommendations of the tariff board with regard to oil country goods. I might tell the committee again that there were increases in some items and decreases in other items but, generally, there was an overbalance toward an increase as compared with a decrease. We had to make concessions with regard to

bread, wax and barytes in order to negotiate the package with our trading partners.
Of course, with a slightly increased tariff one would hope there would be an increase in manufacturing or, at least, a maintenance of the scale upon which these particular goods are manufactured in Canada. However, I think it is impossible to forecast exactly what will happen because so much depends on what will happen in the oil industry itself. If it goes well, then, of course, we believe that manufactures associated with it will continue to expand. Indeed, that probably would be the case without the tariff changes. I should like once again to stress that the oil industry and the manufacturing industry seem to be satisfied with the changes and there have been no complaints to us about them.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, under item 492c machinery and apparatus used in extracting oil from shales and sand will be dutiable at the same rates as similar machinery and apparatus used in connection with oil wells; that is, at rates of 5 per cent British preference and 10 per cent most favoured nation, when of a class or kind made in Canada, and free when not made in Canada. This will provide an incentive for Canadian manufacturers to produce some of this equipment as the demand for it expands, while at the same time affording duty free access to imported equipment of a kind which cannot be obtained in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, would the parliamentary secretary please advise me how the sales tax applies here. Is this one of those items which, if it is imported free of duty, will not attract sales tax, or is it free of sales tax in any event?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I cannot answer that question off the cuff, Mr. Chairman. I shall be pleased to look into the matter for the hon. member. It requires looking into the Excise Tax Act, which is not being considered at the moment. I will look into the matter and advise the hon. member of the position.
Machinery and apparatus of a class or kind not made in Canada for producing unrefined oil from shales was duty free under item 410c (i). If made in Canada, it was dutiable under item 427(1) or 446a at 10 per cent B.P. and 22J per cent M.F.N. Machinery and apparatus for extracting oil from oil sands was duty free under item 410c(ii).
With regard to item 492d, the reason materials entering into these items were made duty free was that in some instances there would have been serious anomalies where items were themselves subject to only a 10 per cent duty when coming into Canada-there was a 10 per cent protection for them in Canada-but

-the goods used to manufacture them would have been coming into this country at varying rates up to 221 per cent. This was really put in to tidy up the tariffs with respect to the items used in the manufacture of these goods.
This was a negotiated item, was it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes, it was a negotiated item within the whole package. The other item mentioned was No. 848, and I should point out in respect of this item that in volume 2 the board recommends free entry for bits not manufactured in Canada, and previously, there were rates of 5 per cent B.P. and 15 per cent M.F.N. on those made.

speechtext: Order. It being five o'clock, the house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely notices of motions.

That, in order to ensure the continuance of the vital part being played by the tobacco industry in the economy of this nation, this house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of providing a much larger grant of money to be used toward research and experimental work in the production and processing of tobacco.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out as briefly as possible the value of tobacco farming to the people of Canada and to those
Tobacco Production Research of Ontario in particular. However, before doing so may I say I have neither direct involvement nor financial interest in the farming, the manufacturing or the distributing of tobacco. However there is one thing that I do have, and that is a direct concern for all the people involved in all these activities. Whether we call it health or whether we call it economic life, just let us remember that we are dealing with people, and people are my immediate responsibility and the responsibility of all members in this house. Until about 40 years ago the sandy wasteland along the northern shores of lake Erie was of little value from an agricultural viewpoint. The provincial governments of that time spent millions of dollars in reforestation programs and reclamation projects. Then in the 1920's tobacco culture started to transform this unproductive land into one of Canada's most prosperous farm areas. Within the last 36 years flue cured tobacco produced in Ontario, and on this land in particular, has increased from some 5 million pounds to close to 200 million pounds. In dollars and cents, it has increased from a $2 million industry to a $100 million industry today.
Just how well this former wasteland is utilized becomes apparent when one considers that flue cured tobacco produces by far the highest farm value per acre. In 1962 it was $788 per acre, which was only exceeded by an all time high of $881 per acre in 1960, compared with $46.50 which is the average for all remaining field crops in Ontario. This works out, by the way, to a ratio of 17 to 1. In all, tobacco accounts for about one fifth of Ontario's gross value of field crops and 10 per cent of the province's total farm cash income from the sale of all farm products.
Canadian tobacco farmers now supply over nine tenths of the basic raw material used by the tobacco products industry, which employs about 10,000 people. I should like to draw attention to the fact that the annual selling value of factory shipments totals approximately $600 million, including excise duties and taxes, the bigger percentage of which, incidentally, flows into the federal tax coffers.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the tobacco industry is the most highly taxed of all industries in the Dominion of Canada. I will not go into detail on this aspect of the industry, but I should like to point out that the federal tobacco taxes provide 7 per cent of the federal budgetary tax. This certainly contrasts very sharply with the picture in the United States, where tobacco taxes provide 2 per cent of the federal budgetary tax revenue. Yet the government of the United States believes that the tobacco industry is so important to the economy of that nation that a multi-million dollar crash
2998	HOUSE OF
Tobacco Production Research program on research to remove health hazards from smoking has won full approval. In comparison, our Department of National Health and Welfare set aside some $200,000 over a five year period, which means about $40,000 a year, which I should think is hardly enough to buy postage stamps to carry on an effective campaign in research.
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member meant to say $600,000, not $200,000.

No, it is $200,000. The other $400,000 has nothing to do with research but is connected with educating the children in schools. I am talking of the research program itself, which is exploring the reasons why people are smoking. The other $400,000 has nothing to do with research in the way I am sure most of us would think of research. However, I will come back to this question a little later on.
In the meantime I should like to bring to the attention of the house some important facts relating to the tobacco industry and to present Your Honour with a few illustrations. I am sure that everyone in this house as well as the people of Canada will agree that the building of the St. Lawrence seaway was a tremendous and courageous task, not only with regard to its construction but also in the raising of the money. Hon. members may ask, what has this to do with the tobacco industry? I would say simply this, that one year's federal excise tax on tobacco would provide 80 per cent of the original cost of the seaway. Or, in dollars and cents, that means something like $400 million a year, or better than $1 million a day.
In these days of demand, both by the government and by the people of Canada, for industry in Canada to be Canadian controlled, it is gratifying to know that here is one industry that is as close to being 100 per cent Canadian operated as can be hoped for. In 1926 Canadian tobacco represented only about one quarter of the cigarette tobacco consumed in this country. Today it is 99 per cent.
Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that tobacco farmers hire some 50,000 seasonal workers and pay them some $35 million a year as wages; and that the use of insecticides and fertilizers by these tobacco farmers runs into millions of dollars annually? Do you realize that there are something like 90,000 retailers selling tobacco throughout the country and doing $130 million worth of business? Do you also realize that 500,000 pounds of string similar to that used by stores to tie up parcels is used by tobacco farmers to tie up their tobacco in the fields? Do you realize, for example, that the provision of cigarette paper alone is a $2 million a year business;


that cellophane is a $3 million a year business; that filters are $6 million a year business; that foil is a $5 million a year business; and that cartons for shipping purposes are a $10 million a year business? I just offer those few thoughts to show the part the tobacco industry is playing in the economy of this country.
Coming back to the farmer himself who grows tobacco, what he and his land means to the community and to the surrounding areas in terms of dollars and cents is astounding. For example, let me take property taxes. I could give a number of examples, but in order to save time I will give only one, that of a general farm situated on light soil. This farm has been owned by the same family for over 100 years. The property tax on that farm is $416. A nearby tobacco farm on similar soil, with only 102 acres-48 acres less-has a property tax of $1,223. In other words, in the case of two farms on similar soil, one a tobacco farm and the other a general farm, the tobacco farm is returning to the community three to four times the amount of tax of the other farm. May I add -and this is ironic-that the man who owns the tobacco farm, which used to be practically waste land, has to go out and work extra hours in order to make a living. His job is that of a carpenter and he has to build tobacco kilns in order to help balance things out a little.
In the tobacco counties of Norfolk and Elgin as well as Essex, Oxford, Brant and Durham, the municipal services which have been provided have been based on the revenue from flue cured tobacco. Without this revenue the counties' whole economic structure would collapse. For example, the debenture issue outstanding would be an impossible burden on the taxpayer. In Norfolk county alone the additional tax on tobacco land, assessments on kilns and greenhouses, and so forth, amount to something like $17.5 million annually. So I am sure you can readily understand, Mr. Speaker, that the impact of tobacco is tremendous both on this and on other communities where tobacco is grown. Tobacco affects every business from the barber to the banker. Said a banker in the town of Tillsonburg: "Around 68 per cent of the business of this town is contingent on tobacco".
May I now deal directly with the motion, which asks that more money be set aside not only for experiment and research in relation to smoking and cancer, but also, and this is very important, at the ground roots level in the production and processing of tobacco under the supervision of the federal experimental farms at Delhi and Harrow, Ontario.

Talking of research, I feel sure that there is a field of research in the tobacco industry that has been given little or no thought, and that is for tobacco to be put to other uses. I should like to see very extensive research done along this line to be sure that this plant cannot be used for other purposes. To a degree it is now. We all know that there are a great many products emanating from industries which have no connection whatever with the original products of these industries. The best example I can think of is the dairy industry; and the best example of that industry is milk. No one would have thought a few years ago that milk, which is babies' food, would be used in the production of plastics. There is a future in everything and we have to give this full consideration.
There is little doubt that in the past few years the tobacco industry's experimental work in Canada has come almost to a standstill. I am talking about the experimental farms at Delhi and Harrow. Other countries were helped to get going in the production of tobacco by the tobacco industry in Canada and by the experimental stations at Delhi and Harrow in particular. Now these countries are moving far ahead of Canada.
One of the best examples I can cite is Rhodesia. The Rhodesian government and growers realize that if the industry is to go ahead they must have the latest information in research along all lines from plant pathology to selling. Because of this belief the experimental station in Rhodesia employs somewhere around 60 people, from top scientists to ordinary help, which is about four times as many as in Canada. These men are working in many different departments such as agronomy, entomology, plant pathology, engineering, which has to do with producing tobacco machinery, soil chemistry and so forth. They are also putting great effort into research at the Rhodesian station in order to sell tobacco. The result is that 90 per cent of the tobacco grown in Rhodesia is sold outside of that country. Even Japan, India and Australia are going ahead by leaps and bounds in the tobacco industry. Australia, with only a quarter of the tobacco acreage that we have in Canada, has as many, if not more, scientists working on tobacco research as are employed at our own experimental farms in Canada.
As the member of parliament for a tobacco county, may I point out that the county of Norfolk produces almost half the tobacco grown in the Dominion of Canada. I feel it is my duty to bring these facts to the attention of the house. However, I should like to add that the Department of Agriculture, under the very able leadership of Hon. Harry Hays, is
Tobacco Production Research giving this situation a thorough check and I have no doubt will be doing something to solve the problem of research in the not too distant future.
All that is required, of course, is money. Where is it going to come from? I do not know, but over the last 10 years the federal governments of Canada received over $3 billion in excise duties and taxes from tobacco. Back in 1952 the amount was $250 million while at the present time it is well over $400 million annually.
These moneys have been used for many purposes by the governments of Canada in the form of subsidies and so forth for many industries ranging from gold mining to agriculture, but they have never been used to any account at all to help the industry from which the moneys were derived. The former government did give backing to the banks so that the growers' organization could have money to process their tobacco, and the present government sent a mission overseas to see what they could do to sell tobacco. It was fairly, but not fully successful. To my knowledge this is all that has been done for the tobacco industry by the various governments over the years.
To those who say that Canada can import tobacco and still receive such taxes I will only say at this time that this is not as practical as it may seem and it will not return the same over-all amount of money. I should like to impress on all members of the house and the government in particular that the fact still remains that the Canadian tobacco industry is the highest taxed industry in Canada. Let us not forget that it is an industry which, if it remains as it is or increases in size, will continue to return to the government of Canada millions of dollars annually not only in the form of taxes but through the over-all economy of the nation itself.
It is certainly to the advantage of the government of Canada to keep such an industry well and flourishing. Therefore, is it not just common sense to take earnings from the business itself and put them to use to better that business? I know that moneys for government projects are taken from the general fund and I realize that this is the only practical way. However, why not base a grant for tobacco research programs on say 5 per cent of the income received by the government from the tobacco industry, which would amount to roughly $200,000 a year, not $200,000 in five years?
In summing up I should like to say that this government or any government cannot afford to let a business such as the tobacco industry go backward without making a real effort to sustain it. There is one way to help it and that is through an effective research

Tobacco Production Research program. Money will be required. The business itself is giving that money to the government. Why not make use of a percentage of it to assist the business? Now, as never before, research is needed in the tobacco industry. Therefore I appeal to the government to see that moneys will be advanced for research and experimental purposes relating to the tobacco industry.

Mr. Speaker, this motion of the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) suggests that the government give more consideration to providing a larger grant of money for research into the production and processing of tobacco. I would suggest that the hon. member should have added a few additional words and included after the word "processing" the words "marketing at home and abroad".
Let us review briefly the Canadian tobacco industry from the production standpoint. The production of tobacco first started in the province of Ontario in the counties of Essex, Kent, Elgin and Norfolk and later was introduced in the counties of Oxford, Brant and Middlesex and many others in the province. The first crops grown were cured by air. The air method of curing is by cutting the whole plant, splitting the stock and hanging it over a lath in a barn with partially open sides to allow the air to circulate around the plant and eventually to cure it. This method is still used in the production of burley tobacco.
By scientific research it was found that tobacco of the flue cured variety could be successfully grown on the more sandy soils in the counties I have mentioned. By this method of production and curing with the use of heat it has been possible to produce in Ontario cigarette tobacco of the finest quality of any country in the world.
Let us look at these areas that now produce this crop, tobacco, as they were previous to 1920 and to the first growing of tobacco crops. I happen to be old enough to remember my visits to the county represented by the hon. member for Norfolk, when a trip by car from my home in St. Thomas to the famous sandhills, a distance of less than 50 miles, was an experience to remember. In those days, on a trip through what is now some of the best tobacco land in the world the roads were only ruts in the sand, and once the wheels of the vehicle entered the ruts it was like being on the rails of a railroad. When you met an oncoming vehicle you had to look for a side track and endeavour to get your vehicle into that siding in order to let the other one pass. Many farms were abandoned, and those who were endeavouring to eke out a living were only able to do so by sacrificing repairs to buildings, fences, bams and so forth.

This county was very familiar to me as a young lad because it was the birthplace of my mother and from her I had learned of the hardships and privations of pioneering in this land that was later to be known as the producer of green gold. The hon. member has referred to land values. In those days land values in the tobacco areas ranged from $10 to $30 per acre, depending on the buildings and the amount of cleared land.
With the coming into production of flue cured tobacco, we find that in the space of less than 40 years a tremendous change has taken place in the complexion of this tobacco growing area. It is quite common today for a tobacco farm fully equipped with kilns, greenhouses, packbarn and other equipment, to sell for $1,000 per acre. As a result of this increase in land values and assessment, municipal councils have been able to show tremendous improvements by providing better roads, new schools, more drainage and so on. We have today some of the finest farms in Canada in the tobacco growing areas of Ontario, and they are a distinct asset to any community.
Tobacco growing has spread to many other areas in eastern Canada. In the province of Quebec the area represented by my colleague, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), is the chief producer of flue cured tobacco. We now learn that several Ontario growers have purchased some
1.000	acres of land near Shawville, about 50 miles northwest of Ottawa, and will be opening up a new area for production next year. Tobacco growing in the maritime provinces is a relatively new industry and is meeting with considerable success, as well as a few failures. Last year Nova Scotia produced
228.000	pounds from 218 acres grown by some eight growers. In New Brunswick seven growers produced tobacco on 120 acres with some increase in production over the previous year. Prince Edward Island has been the largest producer in the maritime provinces and had in production about 450 acres in 1963. It can be seen, therefore, that this is not a regional product but it is grown now and has been grown in six out of the ten provinces. In years past British Columbia has produced small amounts of tobacco. To date, there are over 4,600 farms with rights to produce tobacco in the province of Ontario, or less than 4 per cent of the province's commercial farms. Gross revenues from these farms will exceed $90 million. In other words,
9.5	per cent of Ontario farm cash income was derived from tobacco.
Flue cured acreage has been only about
1.5	per cent of all field crop acreage in Ontario, and the farm value of the tobacco

produced was 20 per cent of the value of all field crops. Farm values per acre produced were more than double that of any other major field crop. Tobacco has been produced in Ontario under strict acreage control methods in order to keep production within the needs of domestic and export requirements. Despite the reduced acreage for each of the last three years, growers have produced over 100 million pounds of tobacco each year. This has occurred as a result of favourable growing conditions, better production methods and better varieties less subject to blight, as well as irrigation and many other factors.
Despite the rosy picture of the past history of tobacco, growers today, on the eve of a new crop year, find themselves faced with a very uncertain future. At the present time some 15 million to 20 million pounds of the 1963 crop has yet to be sold through the auction exchanges. The growers themselves have agreed to cut their acreage by 55 per cent for 1964. The average daily price of around 50 cents per pound has dropped to an average of less than 32 cents. The government has refused to help the tobacco farmers as a result of their request for assisting in processing the unsold tobacco. A support price was put on tobacco, but it is only a moral support since it does not assist the producer by giving him more money for his tobacco. It appears that the support price was placed low enough that the government would not have to spend a penny in supporting this crop. The average price on the crop sold to date is less than 49 cents and unless the average drops to below the 47 cents support price, no money will be paid to the growers.
Now, let us look at the other side of the coin and see the revenue that is derived from the tobacco industry by the government. No other agricultural product is taxed like tobacco at the present time. From each cigarette smoked, the government receives nearly one cent in tax revenue. It is estimated that all forms of tax revenue derived from tobacco net the government around $400 million yearly. I have no hesitation, therefore, in supporting this resolution and further recommending that at least one per cent of the $400 million be set aside as a fund for research and to further export sales of tobacco. This money might also be used, when necessary, to subsidize the export of tobacco.
In 1962 when the Ontario flue cured tobacco growers were having difficulty marketing their crop, the Conservative government helped them to remove unsold tobacco from the market, to have it processed and stored. This surplus tobacco was paid for by government guaranteed bank loans of up to 80
Tobacco Production Research per cent of the grade prices, and assistance was also given with the processing and storing. The growers themselves agreed to deduct one cent per pound from their 1961 crop income to assist in taking this surplus tobacco off the market. Recently the Ontario flue cured tobacco growers' marketing board have allocated $60,000 to promote the export of Ontario tobacco. About $25,000 of this money will be used to hire a tobacco export promoter and to pay his expenses while travelling abroad. I wish to commend the board at this time for initiating sales of tobacco to European and Asian countries, and opening up new markets for Canada not previously enjoyed.
However, the whole tobacco industry is now experiencing difficult times. It was only a few weeks ago that the Imperial Tobacco Company of Canada, the largest and oldest of the tobacco companies in Canada requested the consent of their shareholders to embark upon a non-tobacco business. An official of the company reported to the annual meeting that they have recently laid off 100 employees as a result of the drop in cigarette sales following the publication of the lung cancer report by the surgeon general of the United States. At the same time Imperial reported a 10 per cent drop in profits for 1963, Rothman's Limited, one of the newer cigarette companies, broke its selling record last year in Canada, sold cigarettes to the value of over $61 million and made a net profit of 70 cents a share which was a record for that company.
I know there are other speakers who wish to present their views on this important phase of our agricultural economy. In closing, may I say I hope the government will take this resolution into consideration and immediately introduce legislation to provide the necessary funds to assist this industry to maintain the place it once held, and should still hold, in the economy of Canada.

I do not
hesitate for a moment in rising to support the motion of the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) which is now before the house. The hon. member referred to the vital part being played by the tobacco industry in the economy of this nation, and it is indeed a vital part.
In speaking of this industry I want to refer particularly to the tobacco growers. In my constituency of Brantford a decidedly important part is played in its economy by the tobacco growers. In the township of Burford the total assessment is $6,982,043 for the year 1964, and of this amount a large percentage represents the assessment levied on the tobacco farms in the township. In the township of Oakland the revenue from

Tobacco Production Research the assessment on tobacco farms is similarly high, and in the township of Brantford, surrounding the historic city of Brantford, the tobacco growers contribute a very high percentage to the municipal treasury.
I am told that the highest grade of tobacco grown in Canada is grown in my constituency. I hesitate to estimate what would happen to the economy of my constituency were these growers suddenly deprived of their source of revenue, either by questionable propaganda against tobacco or unfair trade practices. The loss of purchasing power and the loss in investment that might be expected by these growers could be so great as to dislocate the entire economic structure of my constituency.
I have heard it said that we do not need to waste any sympathy on the people engaged in this agricultural enterprise, that they have entered into the agricultural picture only in recent years, that they have made lots of money, and that they grow a product which only injures health. Of these last two allegations, one is false and the other is not yet proven. Tobacco growers have not made lots of money. I will not deny that money may have been made by speculators in the purchase and sale of farms, but not by the growers as such.
The growers have made a livelihood, but when one considers the enormous investments made by individuals, first in the purchase of farm lands, buildings and equipment, and then when one considers the high mortgage indebtedness, the interest on loans from banks and individuals, the hard work, long hours, of whole families, men, women and children, the profit made is surprisingly low. I have said these growers have worked hard, but I must add that their stake in my community is high.
I heartily approve of the government considering any proposal to grant more money to be used for research into the growing of tobacco, toward rendering it as harmless as possible to health, and generally toward assisting in any way this agricultural vocation, the vocation of tobacco growing, as a worthwhile enterprise and pursuit. I strongly support the hon. member's motion. I urge the house to vote for it and to assist this agricultural enterprise from unfair attack and false accusations due to a misunderstanding of recent press releases and statements made by responsible persons in the scientific and medical world.
There is no more highly respected group of individuals in my province than the tobacco growers. They do not want to come crawling to Ottawa asking for financial help. All they want is fair play, and it might be

wise for the government at this time not to engage in a campaign against smoking so much as to assist in more careful research than has hitherto been available.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join the speakers who have preceded me in offering congratulations to the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) for moving the motion now before us.
I believe that all the previous speakers come from Ontario, the province which has been recognized and is still recognized as a great producer of tobacco.
I commend, therefore, the hon. member for Norfolk for introducing this motion whose purpose is to request the federal government to make available a larger amount of money for the tobacco industry, in order to allow for research that will help tobacco growers across Canada.
Mr. Speaker, when one speaks of tobacco in this country, one refers especially to the province of Ontario, which is recognized as the largest producer. But I should like to remind the house that we have also, in the province of Quebec, a few regions which are quite well-known for their tobacco crops and where fine quality tobacco is grown. I refer in particular to my own region and that of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.
In my riding, we find a tobacco co-operative which, being 80 years old, is the oldest in the province of Quebec. Those last few years, unfortunately, we have discovered that tobacco growing is paying less and less and that a good number of farmers seem to be abandoning it more and more.
For instance, Imperial Tobacco, located in Shefford right in the middle of my riding, gives work to approximately 800 people and manufactures all kinds of tobacco products. And, as stated by the hon. member for Norfolk a few minutes ago, the tobacco industry is the most heavily taxed in Canada.
As a matter of fact, 7 per cent of the federal budget is derived from taxes on tobacco, whereas in the United States the federal budget gets only 2 per cent of its revenue from that source. Here, every day, the federal government takes in between $20,000 and $25,000 in excise tax on the various tobacco products manufactured.
All this to say that the hon. member for Norfolk was certainly justified when he stated, supported by figures, that the tobacco industry was the most heavily taxed in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, out of the $400 million paid in the treasury by way of taxes of all sorts on tobacco, only 1 per cent is applied to research, and I entirely support the view of the hon. member for Norfolk who suggested

that the federal government should give higher grants for research in order to help the tobacco industry.
Mr. Speaker, it is recognized that tobacco growers of certain areas of Ontario and Quebec have to solve different problems.
It is a fact that tobacco is grown in Ontario as in Quebec but, on the other hand, neither the soil nor the climate is always the same. Yet, it is possible to grow about the same kind of tobacco. That is why I think that if some areas received more money, it would certainly help solve the problem of the various tobacco growers. It would also help the marketing of all kinds of tobacco products.
Mr. Speaker, I think that it is possible to help the tobacco growers, and what has affected the industry the most recently-though it has not yet been proved, I am told-is the statement that smoking tobacco and cigarettes may be a cause of cancer. That is precisely why I believe that the research council which has been mentioned in this discussion should receive larger grants, in order to put a safe tobacco on the market. Nowadays, cigarette smokers and tobacco consumers are not yet convinced that cigarettes are innocuous in this respect. They still have some doubts on the matter and that affects the tobacco industry.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I feel it is urgent, in view of the well-known publicity and the suspicion prevailing among the public that smoking is the cause of a certain disease, that the government take action in this regard to prevent any more wrong from being done to our tobacco growers who are concerned because they are not sure whether they shall be able to grow tobacco in a few years from now and whether they should improve their methods of tobacco growing. Farmers who specialize in tobacco growing do not know in the least what to do at the present time.
As for me, I agree with the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) who was shrewd and wise enough to introduce such a motion. I hope that the federal government will carry out his suggestions in order to relieve the farmers and to dispel the present confusion in the field of tobacco growing.

May I say at
the outset that I agree with everything said by the previous speakers, including the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) who presented this motion. I do not wish to repeat what other hon. members have said, but I should like to add one or two additional thoughts. I believe that, despite the present criticism of tobacco products, cigarettes in particular, this industry can be expanded in Canada. Since the amount of land available
Tobacco Production Research in the appropriate climatic area of the country is limited, I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Norfolk is an excellent one.
I believe his suggestion would be greatly assisted if the resolution could be referred to a committee of this house, perhaps the standing committee on agriculture, where scientists and agricultural experts could be called as witnesses and outline methods by which the production and processing of tobacco could be improved in this country. I hope consideration will be given to this suggestion.
In addition, I think sales of tobacco products throughout the world could be increased. The Ontario flue cured tobacco marketing board has done a great deal in this regard recently, with assistance from the province of Ontario. Countries behind the iron curtain and in the Middle East have been visited, and I understand there is a possibility of sales of tobacco to those countries. A year or so ago arrangements were made with the government of Japan-and I may say I had something to do with them-for the purchase of Canadian tobacco. Tobacco, in Japan, is a government monopoly. Japan sent representatives to this country and a token purchase of half a million pounds was made. We hope efforts will be continued by the Department of Trade and Commerce to encourage sales to Japan.
There is a good deal more I could say on this subject, but maybe others wish to speak and I shall confine my remarks to the following aspect. There has been great talk about the danger of smoking cigarettes-I have in mind the report of the surgeon general of the United States, and other medical reports, from which it would appear that allegations concerning the dangers of the heavy smoking of cigarettes seem to be correct. As far as lung cancer is concerned, it does seem to produce a hazard to health. As has been pointed out by the previous speaker, the tobacco industry is far too valuable to be allowed to be wiped out by this threat to its existence. In view of the fact that billions of dollars have gone into the federal treasury over the years as a result of taxes on tobacco sales it would seem to me that money should be provided by the government in large sums annually so as to find the alleged cancer-producing substance in tobacco, and discover ways of removing it so that people who like to smoke may continue to do so without this health hazard which does appear to exist.
It is all very well for the government to allocate $400,000 so that the Minister of National Health and Welfare can put out propaganda against cigarette smoking. It would appear much more sensible to me if

Tobacco Production Research that money had been given to research institutions to try to find out ways of removing this cancer-producing substance from cigarettes, in view of the enormous value of this industry to Canada. It is imperative the government should do this. It is difficult for us to know how much should be spent each year on research into this matter and I think the best thing to do would be not only to have this resolution referred to the standing committee on agriculture, but also to the special committee of this house on food and drugs, where witnesses could tell us how research money could best be spent so as to achieve the object I have just mentioned. This work might best be done at the universities or by scientific groups. Perhaps it could best be carried out by commercial groups. In any case, I think it should be done. For this reason I believe the resolution should be referred to both the committees I have named, so that we can find out the best means of undertaking this very necessary research. I fully support the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think this notice of motion is a very important one and one which should receive further study by a committee where witnesses could be called, and so on. If I might have the unanimous consent of the house I will propose an amendment which I believe would have the effect of sending the subject matter of this notice of motion to a standing committee. Perhaps, by unanimous consent, I can move, seconded by my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Benidickson):
That the motion be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the word "nation", and substituting therefor the following:
"The standing committee on agriculture and colonization be empowered to review the research and experimental facilities now provided to the production and processing of tobacco in this country and to recommend such measures as may be expedient to promote and assist in the production of Canadian tobacco."

I am wondering whether the acting leader of the house would not consider making a slight amendment to his amendment so as to refer the subject matter also to the special committee on food and drugs. I agree it should go to the committee on agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I believe that at a later date we might have another motion which would bring about that effect, if such course were thought at that time to be desirable.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. A motion to refer a question to a committee is not normally considered as an amendment.

I would therefore have to consider the hon. member's motion as a substantive motion, and under standing order 44, page 29, unanimous consent would be required. I inquire of the house now whether they give unanimous consent to the hon. member introducing his motion. Is unanimous consent given?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I will be just a few minutes in making these remarks. I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) for introducing this notice of motion and give him credit for having the great amount of courage that it must have taken to introduce into this house a resolution such as this asking his government to give grants to foster and promote the tobacco industry, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) of that government has taken $600,000 of the taxpayers' money in order to try and stop people from smoking. So we have quite a paradox here this afternoon, and I would not want this occasion to pass without bringing to the attention of the hon. member that this paradox exists within his party. I therefore commend him for having the courage to bring this motion before the house.
I speak as one coming from an area that has one of the finest tobacco processing plants on the whole North American continent. I refer to the Imperial Tobacco plant situated in Guelph. The hon. member for Shefford has another plant of Imperial Tobacco in his area. If it were not for the producers of tobacco, this great industry in my riding would not be able to flourish and exist. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Norfolk for having the courage to overcome this paradox that has existed in his party, and I hope that when this matter comes before the committee we will be able to have further discussion on it.

Mr. Speaker, I enter the debate at this late stage only because of the importance of this industry to my part of Ontario. In my area there are four factories that process tobacco. Our county is one of the oldest tobacco growing areas in Canada and this industry is still an

important part of our economy. The hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) has referred to one paradox. I should like to refer to another. I well remember that in 1958 when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was in Brantford, I think, he said they would do something about these unrealistic taxes on tobacco-and they certainly did; the minister of finance raised the taxes on tobacco shortly after that in order to provide more revenue for the govern-
